A wall can push back, and a push is a pressure.

acceptedIdeas: Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water movement depends on both solute concentration and pressure; the simple partition model omits this opposition.

choices.label: The membrane must disappear
Water must keep entering without limit
Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry

questions.onCorrect: Pressure from the wall can reduce or stop net entry of water, so a plant cell does not burst as an animal cell can.

misconceptions.feedback: An opposing pressure is exactly what limits the entry. Once it balances the tendency of water to enter, net entry stops.
The membrane stays in place. The pressure comes from the wall pushing back against the swelling cell.

questions.prompt: Name the energy barrier that an enzyme lowers.
hints: The barrier is the push a reaction needs before it can start.
The word for the push is built from the word 'activate'.
It is a two-word name ending in 'energy'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enzyme provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy.

questions.onCorrect: Activation energy. An enzyme lowers this barrier and does not supply the reaction's energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a kind of energy, but not the barrier the question names. The barrier is the push a reaction needs before it can start.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A's rates at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C are 2, 8, 12 and 3 units per minute. What is the highest rate measured, in units per minute?
hints: Look only at the rates, not at the temperatures.
There are four rates to compare.
Pick the largest of the four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest of 2, 8, 12 and 3 is 12 units per minute, at 40°C.

questions.onCorrect: 12 units per minute, at 40°C. The rate climbs to that point and then falls at 55°C.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the temperature at which the highest rate occurred. The question asks for the rate itself.
That is the rate at 55°C, the last value in the list, which is the second lowest of the four.
That is a temperature. The question asks for the highest of the rates.

questions.prompt: In an enzyme reaction every active site is busy, and adding more substrate no longer raises the rate. Which substance limits the rate?
hints: Think about what has run out of free active sites.
Adding substrate has stopped helping, so substrate is not the limit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fixed amount of enzyme limits how many substrate molecules can be processed at once.

questions.onCorrect: The enzyme. Once every active site is busy, only more enzyme can raise the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: Extra substrate is already in surplus here, which is why adding more makes no difference. Something else is now limiting the rate.

questions.prompt: After 3 minutes, the matched enzyme sample has 27 product units and the control has 9. How many units of product can be credited to the enzyme?
hints: The control shows how much product forms without the enzyme.
The enzyme sample's extra product is the credit the enzyme earns.
Subtract the control's product from the enzyme sample's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 27 − 9 = 18 extra product units in this comparison.

questions.onCorrect: 27 − 9 = 18. The control shows what forms anyway, so only the extra 18 units can be credited to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the enzyme sample's whole product. Some of it would have formed anyway, as the control shows.
That is the control's product, which formed without the enzyme. The question asks for the difference between the two.
Adding the two samples together does not measure the enzyme's effect. Subtract the control from the enzyme sample.

questions.prompt: A high-temperature treatment lowers one enzyme's activity. What is a plausible explanation?
hints: Think about what high temperatures do to a folded protein.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: High temperature can denature an enzyme and disrupt binding or catalysis.

choices.label: Every enzyme works best at that temperature
Heat always increases enzyme activity
Its active-site shape has changed

questions.onCorrect: Its active-site shape has changed. Heat can unfold an enzyme, and the substrate then no longer fits.

misconceptions.feedback: Enzymes differ in the temperature they work best at, so no single temperature suits them all.
Heat speeds an enzyme up only until its shape begins to change. After that it lowers the activity.

questions.prompt: Which experiment best tests an enzyme's effect?
hints: The only difference between the samples should be the thing you are testing.

acceptedIdeas: Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Holding other conditions constant isolates enzyme addition, while replication estimates variability.

choices.label: Compare different organisms at unrelated times
Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition
Change enzyme, temperature and acidity together

questions.onCorrect: Matched, replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition, so any difference can be credited to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: Changing three things at once makes it impossible to say which one caused a difference.
Different organisms at unrelated times differ in many ways besides the enzyme.

questions.prompt: Name the gas that supplies the carbon atoms in a leaf's newly made sugar.
hints: Look at the equation: which input contains carbon?
The carbon does not come from the water, and it is not oxygen.
It is the gas that animals breathe out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide supplies the carbon atoms; light supplies energy.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Its carbon is joined into glucose, and the leaf releases the oxygen.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is released by the leaf, not taken up to build the sugar. The carbon atoms come from another gas.
Water supplies hydrogen and oxygen but contains no carbon. The carbon in the sugar comes from a gas in the air.
Light supplies energy and has no atoms to contribute. The carbon atoms come from a gas in the air.

questions.prompt: One glucose has six carbon atoms. Each CO₂ supplies one. How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for five glucose molecules?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in the glucose that is made.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms and each CO₂ brings one.
Multiply the number of glucose molecules by six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five glucose contain 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, so they need 30 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: Five glucose contain 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, and each CO₂ supplies one, so 30 are needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Six CO₂ would supply the carbon for a single glucose. Five glucose need five times as many.
That is the number of glucose molecules. Each one needs six CO₂, since it contains six carbon atoms.
Adding 5 and 6 does not count the carbon. Each of the five glucose needs six CO₂, so multiply.

questions.prompt: In photosynthesis, in what form is light energy stored?
hints: The light is absorbed, but it does not stay as light.
Think about what the bonds in glucose can store.
The answer is a two-word kind of energy, named for the bonds of molecules.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Photosynthesis captures some incoming light energy as chemical energy in sugar.

questions.onCorrect: Chemical energy, held in the bonds of glucose until a cell releases it.

misconceptions.feedback: Light is the form in which the energy arrives. The question asks for the form in which it is stored.
Some energy does disperse as heat, but what the leaf stores in glucose is a different form.

questions.prompt: A leaf has a low supply of CO₂. Its photosynthetic rate is 8 at light level 60 and 8 at light level 80. By how much did the rate increase?
hints: Read the rate at each light level.
Subtract the earlier rate from the later one.
Ask whether the rate changed at all.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 8 = 0. The curve is flat between those light levels.

questions.onCorrect: The rate did not change: 8 − 8 = 0. With so little CO₂, extra light cannot be used.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in light level, from 60 to 80. The question asks about the change in rate.
That is the rate itself. The question asks by how much it increased.
Adding the two rates does not give an increase. Subtract the earlier rate from the later one.

questions.prompt: A leaf cell has chloroplasts. Name the process, besides photosynthesis, that it uses to transfer energy from sugar.
hints: Photosynthesis does not replace every other cell process.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells also respire to support their energy needs.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. Photosynthesis stores the energy, and respiration releases it for the cell's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the process the question rules out. Name the other one.

questions.prompt: Using the simplified overall equation, how many O₂ molecules accompany the formation of three glucose molecules?
hints: The simplified equation gives the oxygen released for one glucose.
It is the same number as the CO₂ taken in.
Multiply that number by the three glucose.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose corresponds to six O₂: 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: Each glucose is accompanied by six O₂, so three glucose give 3 × 6 = 18.

misconceptions.feedback: Six O₂ accompany a single glucose. Three glucose give three times as many.
That is the number of glucose molecules. Each is accompanied by six O₂.
Adding 3 and 6 does not count the oxygen. Each glucose releases six O₂, so multiply.

questions.prompt: Name the molecule that commonly transfers energy from respiration to cellular work.
hints: It carries energy from where fuel is broken down to where work is done.
Its name is a three-letter abbreviation.
The letters stand for adenosine triphosphate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ATP couples energy-releasing processes to energy-requiring work.

questions.onCorrect: ATP. It carries energy from respiration to the cell's work.

misconceptions.feedback: Glucose is the fuel. The question asks for the molecule that carries energy from the fuel's breakdown to the cell's work.
DNA stores instructions and does not carry energy to the cell's work.
That is a gas taken in or given out. The question asks for the molecule that carries energy within the cell.

questions.prompt: A cell completely breaks down two glucose molecules using oxygen. How many CO₂ molecules does it produce?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in the two glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms, and each CO₂ takes one.
Multiply the number of glucose molecules by six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose contributes six carbon atoms: 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: Two glucose hold 2 × 6 = 12 carbon atoms, and each leaves in its own CO₂, so 12 CO₂ are produced.

misconceptions.feedback: Six CO₂ carry away the carbon of a single glucose. Two glucose give twice as many.
That is the number of glucose molecules. Each one gives six CO₂.
Adding 2 and 6 does not count the carbon. Each of the two glucose gives six CO₂, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A living plant has stored fuel and oxygen but no light. Name the energy-transfer process that can continue.
hints: Which process uses fuel rather than incoming light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Respiration can use stored fuel in darkness even when photosynthesis stops.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. It runs on stored fuel, so it carries on when the light goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Photosynthesis needs light, and there is none. Name the process that uses fuel.

questions.prompt: A sealed jar of living organisms holds 20 units of oxygen at the start and 11 units after three minutes. How many units were consumed?
hints: Compare the oxygen at the start with the oxygen at the end.
The jar began with 20 units.
Subtract the amount at the end from the amount at the start.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 − 11 = 9 oxygen units.

questions.onCorrect: The jar fell from 20 units to 11, so 20 − 11 = 9 units were used.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen left at the end. The question asks how much was used.
That is the oxygen at the start. Some of it was used up, and the question asks how much.
Adding the start and the end does not measure the oxygen used. Subtract the end from the start.

questions.prompt: What happens to glucose's carbon when a cell breaks the glucose down completely using oxygen?
hints: Atoms are rearranged and never lost.
Think about where the carbon of the fuel goes in the equation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose carbon is conserved in CO₂; energy transfer does not destroy those atoms.

choices.label: It becomes only oxygen gas
It vanishes as energy
It appears in carbon dioxide

questions.onCorrect: It appears in carbon dioxide. Energy is released, but the carbon atoms are only rearranged.

misconceptions.feedback: Atoms are never turned into energy in these reactions. The carbon atoms are rearranged into another molecule.
Oxygen gas contains no carbon. The carbon leaves in a different gas.

questions.prompt: Which claim correctly separates breathing from cellular respiration?
hints: One of these moves air and the other happens inside cells.
Think about which one releases energy from fuel.

acceptedIdeas: Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Breathing can supply oxygen, but respiration is a set of chemical processes in cells.

choices.label: Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions
They are exactly the same reaction
Only animals respire

questions.onCorrect: Breathing moves air in and out, and cellular respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that transfer energy from fuel.

misconceptions.feedback: Breathing is the movement of air, not a chemical reaction. Respiration is the set of reactions inside cells.
Plants and bacteria respire too, because every living cell needs energy from fuel.

questions.prompt: A new DNA base is placed opposite adenine (A). Give the name of the base that pairs with it.
hints: Each base has exactly one partner.
The pairs are A with T and C with G.
The partner of adenine begins with the letter T.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adenine pairs with thymine in standard DNA base pairing.

questions.onCorrect: Thymine. Adenine always pairs with thymine, and cytosine with guanine.

misconceptions.feedback: Guanine and cytosine pair with each other. Adenine has a different partner.
A base does not pair with its own kind. Adenine's partner is a different base.
Uracil takes thymine's place in a different nucleic acid. In DNA, adenine has another partner.

questions.prompt: Write the partner bases beneath the strand 5′-AAGC-3′, from left to right.
hints: Pair each base in turn, from the left.
The pairs are A with T and C with G.
The first two bases are both A, so the first two partners are alike.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so AAGC is matched by TTCG.

questions.onCorrect: TTCG. A takes T, G takes C and C takes G, base by base.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strand you were given. The partner strand has a different base opposite each one.
C is the partner of G, not of A. Pair each base with its own partner: A with T, and C with G.
The order is reversed. Write the partners from left to right, in the same order as the strand.

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA molecule replicates once. How many double-stranded DNA molecules result?
hints: Each of the two old strands is used as a template.
Each template gets a new strand built against it.
Every new molecule is one old strand paired with one new strand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One molecule is copied into two, each with one old and one new strand.

questions.onCorrect: Two. Each old strand serves as a template, so one molecule becomes two with an old and a new strand apiece.

misconceptions.feedback: Replication produces a second molecule. One molecule becomes more than one, each made from one of the old strands.
Each old strand is paired with one new strand, which makes two molecules from the one that began.

questions.prompt: A cell has 4 chromosomes before copying. Immediately after copying, while sister chromatids remain joined, how many chromosomes does it have?
hints: Think about what is counted as one chromosome after copying.
The two sister chromatids stay joined and count together.
Compare the number of chromosomes before and after.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It still has four chromosomes; each now has two sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Four. Copying doubles the DNA molecules, but joined sister chromatids still count as one chromosome.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the DNA molecules, one in each chromatid. Joined sister chromatids are counted as a single chromosome.
Copying does not halve the count. The chromosomes are still there, each now made of two chromatids.

questions.prompt: What does semiconservative replication keep in each resulting DNA molecule?
hints: Trace the two original strands separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each resulting molecule pairs an original template strand with a newly made strand.

choices.label: No original material
Both original strands together
One original strand

questions.onCorrect: One original strand, paired with a new one. Each molecule is half old and half new.

misconceptions.feedback: The two original strands separate. Each ends up in a different molecule.
Every old strand is reused as a template, so each new molecule contains one.

questions.prompt: Six chromosomes each have two sister chromatids after copying. How many DNA molecules are present?
hints: Each sister chromatid contains one DNA molecule.
Each of the six chromosomes has two chromatids.
Multiply the number of chromosomes by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each chromatid contains one DNA molecule: 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the six chromosomes holds two chromatids, and each chromatid is one DNA molecule: 6 × 2 = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts chromosomes. Each chromosome now holds two DNA molecules, one in each chromatid.
Adding 6 and 2 does not count the molecules. Each chromosome holds two, so multiply.
Dividing the chromosomes by two goes the wrong way. Copying doubles the DNA molecules.

questions.prompt: Name the nuclear division process used in ordinary tissue growth and repair.
hints: It keeps the starting chromosome number.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mitosis distributes copied chromosomes to daughter nuclei during regulated growth and repair.

questions.onCorrect: Mitosis. It shares copied chromosomes so each daughter nucleus gets a full set.

misconceptions.feedback: Meiosis makes sex cells and halves the chromosome number. Growth needs the full number kept.

questions.prompt: A cell has 6 chromosomes before replication. How many DNA molecules does it have after replication but before mitosis?
hints: The chromosome count does not change when the DNA is copied.
Each chromosome now holds two DNA molecules, one in each sister chromatid.
Multiply the number of chromosomes by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six replicated chromosomes have two chromatids each: 12 DNA molecules.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the six chromosomes now holds two DNA molecules, so there are 6 × 2 = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts chromosomes, which copying leaves unchanged. Each chromosome now holds two DNA molecules.
Adding 6 and 2 does not count the molecules. Each chromosome holds two, so multiply.
Dividing by two goes the wrong way. Copying doubles the number of DNA molecules.

questions.prompt: A cell starts with 4 chromosomes and completes normal mitosis and cytokinesis. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
hints: Ask what mitosis does to the number of chromosomes.
The chromatids of each chromosome are pulled apart and shared out equally.
Each daughter cell gets a complete set, identical to the cell it came from.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each daughter retains the original four chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: Four. Mitosis gives each daughter cell a full set, so the chromosome number is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: Eight is the number of chromatids just before division. Each daughter receives one chromatid of every chromosome.
Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number. Each daughter receives a complete set, as the parent cell had.

questions.prompt: One cell completes three ideal rounds of division, with every cell dividing in every round. How many cells result?
hints: Each round doubles the number of cells.
Start with one cell and double it once for each round.
Double three times in a row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.

questions.onCorrect: Each round doubles the count: 1, 2, 4, then 8 cells after three rounds.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 in each round. Every cell divides, so the count doubles in each round and not grows by a fixed amount.
That is the number of rounds. The question asks for the number of cells.
Squaring the number of rounds is not the rule. Each round doubles the cells present.

questions.prompt: Name the two joined copies of a replicated chromosome that separate during mitosis.
hints: After copying, each chromosome consists of two identical halves.
The halves are joined until mitosis pulls them apart.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sister chromatids separate and become daughter chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They separate in mitosis, and each becomes a chromosome of a daughter cell.

misconceptions.feedback: Together the two copies are counted as one chromosome. The question asks for the name of each joined copy.
Homologous chromosomes come from different parents. These copies come from one chromosome.

questions.prompt: Does a normal body cell divide only because it is about to die?
hints: Separate regulated division from cell death.

acceptedIdeas: No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cell-cycle regulation responds to conditions and signals; imminent death is not the general cause.

choices.label: Yes, and the DNA need not be copied
Yes, that is the defining trigger
No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs

questions.onCorrect: No. Division is regulated and happens when the body needs new cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Cells divide when growth or repair needs them to. Dying is not the trigger.
DNA is always copied first. Without a copy, a daughter would lack half its instructions.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does it contain before DNA replication?
hints: Each homologous pair contains two chromosomes.
There are three pairs.
Multiply the number of pairs by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three pairs contain 3 × 2 = 6 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the three pairs has two chromosomes, one from each parent, so the cell has 3 × 2 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. Each pair contains two chromosomes.
Replication would double the DNA molecules but not the chromosomes, and the question asks for the count before it. Count two chromosomes in each pair.
Adding does not count the chromosomes. Each pair has two, so multiply the number of pairs by two.

questions.prompt: Name the paired chromosomes that are pulled apart in meiosis I.
hints: Meiosis I separates whole chromosomes from one another, not their halves.
It separates the two members of each pair, one from each parent.
The name begins with 'homologous'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate first; sister chromatids remain joined.

questions.onCorrect: Homologous chromosomes. The two members of each pair go to different cells, which is what halves the chromosome number.

misconceptions.feedback: Sister chromatids stay joined through the first division. The structures pulled apart in meiosis I are whole chromosomes.
Gametes are the cells that result at the end. The question asks which structures are pulled apart.

questions.prompt: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. After the two meiotic divisions, how many chromosomes does each final cell have?
hints: Count the number of chromosomes in each final cell, not in the starting cell.
Each final cell receives one chromosome from each pair.
There are two pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each final haploid cell has one from each pair: two chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: Each final cell receives one chromosome from each of the two pairs, so it has 2 chromosomes, half the starting number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number in the starting cell. The two divisions of meiosis halve it.
Each final cell receives one chromosome from every pair, and there are two pairs, so it receives more than one.
Eight would be the number of DNA molecules just after copying. The question asks for the chromosomes in each final cell.

questions.prompt: Two gametes each contain 3 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in their diploid fertilisation product?
hints: Fertilisation combines the two sets.
Each gamete supplies three chromosomes.
Add the two contributions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 + 3 = 6 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Two haploid sets combine to restore a diploid cell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one gamete's contribution. Fertilisation brings two together.
Each gamete supplies three, so add only those two amounts.

questions.prompt: How many additional DNA-replication rounds normally occur between meiosis I and meiosis II?
hints: Trace the copied chromosomes through both divisions.
Meiosis begins with one replication round.
Between the divisions, the DNA is divided again without being recopied.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No additional replication occurs; the second division separates existing sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The second division separates the copies already made, so the amount of DNA halves again.

misconceptions.feedback: That round happens once, before meiosis I. None happens between the divisions.
Each division is a separation, not a copying.

questions.prompt: Why can siblings inherit different chromosome combinations?
hints: Siblings have the same two parents.
Think about what meiosis does to the chromosomes of each pair.

acceptedIdeas: Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assortment and crossing over produce varied gametes; the simple count diagram omits crossover.

choices.label: Each parent has no genetic variation
Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
Fertilisation always uses identical gametes

questions.onCorrect: Chromosomes assort at random and exchange segments in meiosis, so every gamete, and every child, is a new combination.

misconceptions.feedback: Each parent carries two different versions of many genes, which is the variation that meiosis shuffles.
Gametes from one parent are not identical, because meiosis shuffles the chromosomes differently each time.

questions.prompt: What term describes the Aa parent, which carries two different alleles at this gene?
hints: Look at the two letters in Aa.
They are different, one capital and one small.
The word begins with 'hetero', which means different.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aa is heterozygous; its two different alleles can separate into gametes.

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygous. Aa carries two different alleles, while AA and aa each carry two of the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Homozygous means two identical alleles, as in AA or aa. Aa carries two different ones.
Dominant and recessive describe how an allele behaves. The question asks for the name of a genotype with two different alleles.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to have genotype aa?
hints: Draw the four boxes of the square, with the two parents' gametes along its edges.
Each box is one equally likely pairing.
Count the boxes that read aa, and divide by four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One of four equally likely pairings is aa: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

questions.onCorrect: Each parent passes on a with probability one half, so one of the four boxes is aa, which is 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of offspring that carry at least one A. The question asks only for aa, which needs a from both parents.
That is the share of Aa offspring, which receive a from just one parent. The aa genotype needs a from both.
Each offspring has a chance of receiving a from each parent, not a certainty. Count the aa boxes in the square.

questions.prompt: With A completely dominant, which genotypes have the dominant phenotype?
hints: Keep genotype letters separate from the expressed trait.

acceptedIdeas: Two dominant alleles, or one of each
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One A allele is enough for the dominant phenotype in this model.

choices.label: No alleles at this gene
Two dominant alleles, or one of each
Only two recessive alleles

questions.onCorrect: AA and Aa both. One dominant allele is enough to show the dominant trait.

misconceptions.feedback: Two recessive alleles give the recessive trait. Look for the genotypes that hide it.
Every organism has two alleles at the gene, so one of the options must apply.

questions.prompt: Four offspring are produced from Aa × Aa. Which statement is justified?
hints: Each seed is a separate fertilisation.
The result for one seed does not change the chance for the next.

acceptedIdeas: Each has a 25% chance of being aa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Independent random outcomes do not enforce a fixed family quota.

choices.label: Each has a 25% chance of being aa
Exactly one must be aa
None can be aa

questions.onCorrect: Each offspring has a 25% chance of being aa. Chance applies to each one separately and does not promise a family ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: A chance of 25% says how likely each seed is to be aa. It does not guarantee that any set of four contains exactly one.
Both parents carry a, so each seed has some chance of receiving it from both.

questions.prompt: For Aa × aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to show the recessive phenotype?
hints: Draw the square with Aa gametes along one edge and aa gametes along the other.
The aa parent can pass on only a.
Count the aa boxes, and divide by four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two of four equally likely pairings are aa: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.

questions.onCorrect: The aa parent always passes a and the Aa parent passes a half the time, so 2 of the 4 boxes are aa, which is 50%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share for a cross of two Aa parents. Here one parent is aa and always passes on a, so the chance is greater.
The Aa parent passes on A half the time, and those offspring show the dominant trait. Not all of them are aa.
The Aa parent carries a and the aa parent always passes it on, so some offspring will receive a from both.

questions.prompt: In this model, Aa and AA share a phenotype. What term describes A relative to a?
hints: In Aa the trait shows as if only one allele were there.
The allele that shows in Aa has a name that means 'in charge'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A is dominant in this genotype-to-phenotype relationship; that does not establish its frequency or fitness effect.

questions.onCorrect: Dominant. A dominant allele shows its trait whether the other allele is the same or different.

misconceptions.feedback: Recessive is the other allele, the one hidden in Aa. A is the one whose trait shows.
Those words describe a genotype. The question asks how the allele A behaves relative to a.

questions.prompt: ATCG changes to ATGG without changing length. Name this type of single-base change.
hints: The length stays the same, so no base was added or removed.
One base has been swapped for another.
The name begins with 'sub', as in a substitute teacher.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The third base was substituted: C became G.

questions.onCorrect: A substitution. One base is replaced by another, so the length of the sequence does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: An insertion adds a base and makes the sequence longer. Here the length is unchanged.
A deletion removes a base and makes the sequence shorter. Here the length is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Compare AATG with AACG. How many displayed positions differ?
hints: Line the two sequences up and compare them one position at a time.
Mark each position where the letters differ.
Count the marks.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only position three differs: T became C.

questions.onCorrect: Only position three differs, where T has become C, so the count is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: The two sequences are not the same. Compare them position by position and one letter differs.
Check each position again. Only one position has a different letter.
That is the length of each sequence. The question asks how many positions differ.

questions.prompt: Name the reproductive cell type that can carry a DNA mutation directly into an offspring at fertilisation.
hints: Think about which cells pass DNA to a child.
A child begins as a fertilised egg.
The cells are sperm and egg, which together are called by one word.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A contributing gamete can carry a DNA variant into the offspring.

questions.onCorrect: A gamete. A mutation in an egg or sperm is in the cell that becomes the first cell of a child.

misconceptions.feedback: A mutation in a body cell stays in that cell and the cells that divide from it. It is not in the cells that make a child.
A zygote is the first cell of the child, after fertilisation. The question asks for the cell that carries the mutation into it.

questions.prompt: A useful variant becomes more frequent after an environmental change. Which explanation avoids a directed-mutation error?
hints: Mutations arise by chance.
The variants were already there before the environment changed.

acceptedIdeas: Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection can change the frequency of existing variants; need does not direct a specific helpful mutation.

choices.label: Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
Organisms created exactly the mutation they needed
Every individual rewrote its DNA on purpose

questions.onCorrect: Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success, so the useful variant left more offspring.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutations arise by chance and not because they are needed. The change in frequency comes from differences in reproductive success.
No organism rewrites its DNA on purpose. The variants were already in the population.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from a single DNA substitution alone?
hints: A changed letter does not specify a phenotype.

acceptedIdeas: Its biological effect needs additional evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Effects depend on sequence context and environment; some substitutions have little detectable effect.

choices.label: It must be harmful
Its biological effect needs additional evidence
It must improve survival

questions.prompt: Compare the aligned sequences TCGATA and TCAACA. How many positions differ?
hints: Keep both sequences aligned.
Check each of the six positions in turn.
Count the mismatched pairs only.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 3 and 5 differ; the other four agree.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Positions 3 and 5 disagree, so two bases have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: There is another mismatch. Check every position.
That is the length of the sequences. Count only the positions that differ.

questions.prompt: 10 of 40 organisms carry the blue variant. What percentage is blue?
hints: Frequency compares the number with the variant to the whole population.
Divide the number of blue organisms by the total, then convert to a percentage.
Multiply the result by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The blue organisms are 10 out of 40, and 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of blue organisms. The frequency is a share of the whole population, written as a percentage.
That counts the organisms that are not blue, 30 of the 40. The question asks for the blue share.
That divides the total by the blue number. The frequency is the blue number divided by the total, times 100.

questions.prompt: Heritable variants consistently leave different numbers of reproducing descendants. Name the evolutionary process described.
hints: The variants differ in how many offspring they leave.
The differences pass from parents to offspring.
The name is two words, and the first is 'natural'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Natural selection changes frequencies through differences in reproductive success associated with heritable traits.

questions.onCorrect: Natural selection. Heritable variants that leave more offspring become more common over generations.

misconceptions.feedback: Drift is a change due to chance sampling, not to consistent differences in reproduction. The question describes consistent differences.
Mutation produces new variants. The process described is the sorting of existing variants by reproductive success.
Evolution is the wider change in populations over time. The question asks for the process that is driven by differences in reproductive success.

questions.prompt: Blue organisms increase from 15 of 50 to 30 of 50. By how many percentage points does the blue frequency rise?
hints: Work out the blue frequency before and after.
Each is a number out of 50.
Subtract the earlier percentage from the later one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frequency rises from 30% to 60%, a 30-point increase.

questions.onCorrect: The blue frequency rises from 30% to 60%, which is an increase of 30 percentage points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the increase in the number of organisms. The question asks about the change in the percentage.
That is the percentage change in the number of blue organisms. The question asks for the difference between the two frequencies, in percentage points.
That is the frequency after the change. The question asks how far it rose from the earlier one.

questions.prompt: A small population's variant frequency changes. Is selection the only possible cause?
hints: Think about other ways the numbers in a small population can change.
A change in frequency shows that something happened, but not by itself what.

acceptedIdeas: No, chance and migration can also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several evolutionary processes can change frequency; causal evidence is needed.

choices.label: No, chance and migration can also matter
No population can change
Yes, every frequency shift proves selection

questions.onCorrect: Chance and migration can change frequencies too, so the shift alone does not show selection.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift in frequency can also come from chance or from individuals moving in or out. Selection needs evidence of differences in reproductive success.
Populations do change over generations, and the change has several possible causes.

questions.prompt: A once-useful trait becomes disadvantageous after a habitat change. Is this compatible with natural selection?
hints: Think about what an advantage depends on.
A change of habitat changes which variants do well.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection depends on how traits affect reproduction in the current environment.

choices.label: Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment
No, useful traits are always useful
Only if the organism chooses it

questions.onCorrect: Reproductive advantage depends on the environment, so a trait that helped in one habitat can hinder in another.

misconceptions.feedback: A trait is useful or not depending on the environment. When the habitat changes, the advantage can change with it.
Organisms do not choose their heritable traits. Selection acts on differences in reproductive success.

questions.prompt: A later population has 18 blue and 42 gold organisms. What percentage is blue?
hints: Find the total number of organisms first.
Divide the blue number by the total.
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of blue organisms. The question asks for their share of the population, as a percentage.
That divides by the number of gold organisms only. The total includes the blue ones as well.
That is the share that is gold. The question asks for the blue share.

questions.prompt: What does the arrow Grass → Grasshopper mean?
hints: Follow the direction of matter and energy transfer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arrows run from food to consumer.

choices.label: Grass turns directly into a hawk
Grasshoppers obtain food from grass
Grass eats grasshoppers

questions.onCorrect: The grasshopper eats the grass. An arrow runs from the food to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the arrow backwards. It points to whichever organism is doing the eating.
An arrow shows eating, not turning into another organism.

questions.prompt: A pond web has algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron. Which of these is the producer?
hints: A producer builds its own food from light.
A producer does not eat other organisms.
Algae, not the animals, are the ones that photosynthesise.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Algae build organic matter using light; the other organisms consume other organisms.

questions.onCorrect: Algae. They make their own food by photosynthesis, so every route through the pond starts with them.

misconceptions.feedback: That organism eats other organisms, so it is a consumer. A producer makes its own food from light.

questions.prompt: In a meadow web, a hawk eats mice and frogs. Frogs eat grasshoppers, which eat grass. How many direct food sources does the hawk have?
hints: A direct food source is an organism with an arrow pointing to the hawk.
Count only the arrows that end at the hawk.
Arrows that leave other organisms but do not reach the hawk do not count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two arrows enter the hawk: one from mouse and one from frog.

questions.onCorrect: Two arrows end at the hawk, one from mouse and one from frog, so it has two direct food sources.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the grasshopper too, but the grasshopper's arrow ends at the frog. Only arrows that end at the hawk count.
More than one arrow ends at the hawk. Check each organism that the hawk eats.
That counts every organism in the chain below the hawk. A direct food source is one whose arrow ends at the hawk.

questions.prompt: Energy flows through ecosystems and becomes less available for further biological work. In what form does much of it disperse?
hints: Every organism uses energy to stay alive.
Respiration transfers some energy to ATP and disperses the rest.
It is the form of energy that keeps animals warm.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy disperses as heat; atoms can be recycled through environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Energy passes along the arrows but much of it is lost as heat, and it does not return.

misconceptions.feedback: That is not the form in which spare energy leaves a living thing. The form is the one that keeps a mammal's body warm.

questions.prompt: In a meadow food web the number of mice goes down. Can the diagram give an exact future number of hawks?
hints: A web shows which organisms eat which, not how many.
Other foods and conditions can matter as well.

acceptedIdeas: No, other food sources and conditions also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A feeding web shows relationships, not a complete quantitative population model.

choices.label: Yes, arrows specify exact population changes
No, other food sources and conditions also matter
Yes, every hawk must disappear

questions.onCorrect: No. The arrows show who eats whom and not by how much, and other foods and conditions also affect the hawk.

misconceptions.feedback: Arrows show that a feeding link exists. They carry no information about amounts, so they cannot give an exact number.
The hawk has another food source, and other conditions matter too, so a fall in the mice does not mean that every hawk must go.

questions.prompt: A pond web is a chain of algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron, plus one extra link where the heron also eats zooplankton directly. How many feeding links does the web have in total?
hints: Count each arrow once.
The chain has algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron.
A chain of four organisms has links between each neighbouring pair, and then there is one extra link.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain has 3 links, and the extra link makes 4.

questions.onCorrect: The chain of four organisms has 3 links, and the heron's direct link to the zooplankton makes 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the chain. The heron also eats the zooplankton directly, which is a fourth link.
Count each arrow once. A chain of four organisms has three links, plus the one extra.
A chain of four organisms has more than two links, and there is an extra one besides.

questions.prompt: The producers in a habitat hold 1000 kJ of energy. At an assumed transfer efficiency of 10%, how many kJ reach the next level?
hints: Ten percent means one tenth.
The producers hold 1000 kJ.
Multiply 1000 by 0.10.
questions.onCorrect: Ten percent of 1000 kJ is 1000 × 0.10 = 100 kJ, which is what reaches the next level.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy held by the producers. Only a tenth of it reaches the next level.
That is the energy that does not pass on. The question asks for the energy that reaches the next level.
That is the percentage, not an amount of energy. Take ten percent of the 1000 kJ.

questions.prompt: The producers hold 2000 kJ. At an assumed 10% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 3?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Take 10% of the energy once, then take 10% of the result.
Multiply by 0.1 twice.
questions.onCorrect: The first step gives 2000 × 0.1 = 200 kJ and the second gives 200 × 0.1 = 20 kJ at level 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2, after one step. Level 3 is a further step on.
That is the energy held by the producers. Two steps with 10% transfer reduce it a good deal.
That subtracts 10% instead of taking 10%. At each step only a tenth of the energy passes on.

questions.prompt: With 5000 kJ at producers and a 20% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 2?
hints: The stated transfer is 20%, which is 0.20.
Level 2 is one step above the producers.
Multiply 5000 by 0.20.
questions.onCorrect: Twenty percent of 5000 kJ is 5000 × 0.20 = 1000 kJ at level 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ten percent of the energy. This question states a transfer of twenty percent.
That is the energy that does not pass on. The question asks for the energy that reaches level 2.
That is the energy held by the producers. Only a fifth of it reaches level 2.

questions.prompt: A consumer level is to receive 300 kJ. At an assumed 10% transfer, how many kJ must the level below hold?
hints: The level below supplies the energy, and only a tenth of it reaches the consumer level.
The consumer level holds one tenth of what the level below held.
Divide 300 by 0.10.
questions.onCorrect: The consumers receive a tenth of what the level below holds, so that level held 300 ÷ 0.10 = 3000 kJ.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes a tenth of the 300 kJ, which goes up a step and not down one. The level below held more than the consumers received.
That is the energy the consumer level is to receive. The level below must hold more than that.
Adding ten percent is not the reverse of taking ten percent. The level below held ten times what the consumers receive.

questions.prompt: Does every real food web transfer exactly 10% between levels?
hints: Think about whether the 10% was measured or assumed.
Real food webs differ.

acceptedIdeas: No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ten-percent value is a useful stated approximation, not an exact universal constant.

choices.label: No, energy is always fully transferred
No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
Yes, without exception

questions.onCorrect: No. Efficiency varies between food webs and levels, so a calculation has to state it or measure it.

misconceptions.feedback: Measured efficiencies differ from one food web and one level to the next. Ten percent is only a convenient round figure.
Much of the energy at each level is lost, mainly as heat, so it is never fully transferred.

questions.prompt: A fourth level is three steps above producers. From 8000 kJ with an assumed 10% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 4?
hints: Level 4 is three steps above the producers.
Take 10% three times in a row.
Multiply by 0.1 three times.
questions.onCorrect: Each step takes a tenth: 8000 gives 800, then 80, then 8 kJ at level 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 3, after two steps. Level 4 is a further step on.
That is the energy at level 2, after one step. Level 4 needs three steps.
That subtracts 10% three times over a total, which is not how transfer works. Each step passes on a tenth of the energy it begins with.

questions.prompt: A population starts at 10 and doubles each round. What is it after three rounds?
hints: Double once per round.
After two rounds there are 40.
Double once more.
questions.onCorrect: 80. Each round doubles the last, so the increases grow larger.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 10 each round. Each round doubles instead.
That is the count after only two rounds.

questions.prompt: A population grows quickly at first and then levels off. What is the name for the size of population that its habitat can keep supporting?
hints: The size is a limit set by the habitat and not by the population itself.
It is the largest population the habitat can keep supporting.
The name has two words, and the second is 'capacity'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity reflects the population supported by those conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Carrying capacity. Growth slows as the population nears the size its habitat can support.

misconceptions.feedback: You have described the idea. Give the term for the size of population that a habitat can keep supporting.
Those describe how a population grows. The question asks for the size the habitat can support.

questions.prompt: A closed population has 12 births and 12 deaths in one interval. What is its net change?
hints: Net change is the difference between births and deaths.
Births add to the population and deaths take away from it.
Subtract the deaths from the births.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 12 = 0, although individuals were born and died.

questions.onCorrect: Births and deaths cancel, so the net change is 12 − 12 = 0, although the individuals themselves have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of births, or of deaths, on its own. The net change compares the two.
Adding births and deaths does not give the net change, because deaths subtract. Subtract deaths from births.

questions.prompt: After a drought reduces the food supply, what may happen to the carrying capacity?
hints: Think about what carrying capacity depends on.
A drought reduces the food supply.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity depends on environmental resources and conditions.

choices.label: It must remain fixed forever
It becomes the same for every species
It can decrease

questions.onCorrect: It can decrease. The carrying capacity depends on resources, and a drought reduces the food supply.

misconceptions.feedback: Carrying capacity depends on resources such as food and water, so it changes when they change.
Each species depends on different resources, so its carrying capacity differs from other species' in the same habitat.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 70, with 16 births and 9 deaths. What is its final size?
hints: The new size is the starting size plus births minus deaths.
The starting size is 70.
Add the 16 births and take away the 9 deaths.
questions.onCorrect: The population begins at 70, gains 16 and loses 9, so it ends at 70 + 16 − 9 = 77.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the births but does not take away the deaths. Deaths reduce the population.
That takes away both the births and the deaths. Births add to the population.
That is the net change, births minus deaths. The question asks for the final size, which includes the starting 70.

questions.prompt: Does a smooth S-shaped curve predict every fluctuation in a wild population?
hints: The curve is a simplified model of growth.
Real populations also face weather, other species and chance.

acceptedIdeas: No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The curve is a simplified model; real populations can fluctuate or overshoot.

choices.label: Only for populations above one million
Yes, exactly
No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures

questions.onCorrect: No. A smooth curve is a model, and weather, interactions with other species and chance cause departures from it.

misconceptions.feedback: A smooth curve is a simplified model, and real populations rise and fall for reasons the curve does not include.
The size of a population does not make a smooth curve exact. Weather and interactions affect populations of every size.

questions.prompt: A claim says fertiliser helps plants grow. Which measurement would let you test it?
hints: The claim is about growth, so choose something that changes as a plant grows.
It must be something you can measure with a ruler or a balance.

acceptedIdeas: The height of each plant in centimetres, at the start and at the end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The height of each plant in centimetres, at the start and at the end

choices.label: The amount of fertiliser each pot receives
The height of each plant in centimetres, at the start and at the end
How healthy the plants look

questions.onCorrect: Height can be measured the same way on every plant, and measuring it at the start as well as the end shows how much each one grew.

misconceptions.feedback: How healthy a plant looks is a judgement that two people can disagree about. A test needs a quantity that a ruler or a balance can give.
The amount of fertiliser is the thing being tested. The measurement has to be taken on the plants, to see whether they grew more.

questions.prompt: Group A grows from 10 cm to 16 cm. How much does its mean height increase, in cm?
hints: Use the same group's baseline.
Subtract the starting height from the final height.
Take the starting height off the final height.
questions.onCorrect: 6 cm. Growth is the final height minus the baseline.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final height. Subtract the starting height.
That adds the heights. Growth is the change, so subtract.

questions.prompt: Comparable pots are allocated to fertiliser or control by chance. Name this allocation method.
hints: The pots are not picked by the experimenter.
Chance decides which pots get which treatment.
The name has two words, and the first is 'random'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment reduces systematic group differences; independent pots provide replication.

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment. Chance makes the groups alike on average, so a later difference can be put down to the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: A control is the group that gets no treatment. The question asks for the method of allocating pots to groups.
Replication means repeating with several pots. The question asks for the method by which pots are allocated.

questions.prompt: Taller plants occur at wetter sites. What follows from that observation alone?
hints: Think about what else could differ between wet sites and dry ones.
A pattern across sites does not show which way the cause runs.

acceptedIdeas: Rainfall and height are associated, but other causes need checking
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The association could reflect rainfall, soil or other related factors.

choices.label: Rainfall and height are associated, but other causes need checking
Rainfall is proven to be the only cause
Height causes all rainfall

questions.onCorrect: Rainfall and height are associated, but other causes need checking. Wetter sites may also differ in soil or shade.

misconceptions.feedback: An association alone cannot show that rainfall is the only cause. Wet sites may differ in other ways as well.
Nothing in the observation suggests that height changes the rainfall. The association does not show cause in either direction.

questions.prompt: A treated group increases by 9 cm and its control group by 6 cm over the same interval. What is the difference in growth, in cm?
hints: Each group's growth is already given.
The control group shows how much growth happens anyway.
Subtract the control's growth from the treated group's growth.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 6 = 3 cm greater growth in the treated group.

questions.onCorrect: The treated group grew 9 cm and the control 6 cm, so the treatment accounts for 9 − 6 = 3 cm more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treated group's growth on its own. Part of it would have happened without the treatment, as the control shows.
That is the control group's growth, which happened without the treatment. The question asks for the difference between the groups.
Adding the two growths does not measure the treatment's effect. Subtract the control's growth from the treated group's.

questions.prompt: Why report variability across independent pots as well as the mean?
hints: A mean hides how far the individual values spread.
Think about what the spread tells you about the replicates.

acceptedIdeas: It shows how consistent the results are
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variability reveals whether the mean hides wide differences between replicates.

choices.label: It shows how consistent the results are
It makes a control unnecessary
It proves every plant behaves identically

questions.onCorrect: It shows how consistent the results are. A mean with a wide spread is a less reliable guide than one with a narrow spread.

misconceptions.feedback: Variability tells you about the spread among replicates. A control is still needed to show what would have happened without the treatment.
Variability exists because plants differ. Reporting it shows how much, and it does not prove that they behave identically.

questions.prompt: An old strand reads ATGC. Write the bases of the new strand built against it, in the same left-to-right order.
hints: Match each old base with its partner, in order.
The pairs are A with T and C with G.
Write the partners from left to right.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pairing each base in turn gives TACG.

questions.onCorrect: TACG. Each old base is matched in turn: A with T, T with A, G with C and C with G.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old strand itself. The new strand has the partner of each base.
The order is reversed. Write the new strand's bases from left to right, in the same order as the old strand.
One of the partners is wrong. Check each base: A with T, and C with G.

questions.prompt: A template strand has 40 bases. How many bases are in the new strand built against it?
hints: Every template base receives one partner.
A new strand is built along the whole template.
The new strand is as long as the template.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each template base gets exactly one partner, so the new strand also has 40 bases.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 40 template bases gets exactly one partner, so the new strand also has 40 bases.

misconceptions.feedback: Only half would be matched in that case. Every template base gets a partner, so the strands are the same length.
The two strands together hold 80 bases, but the question asks about the new strand alone.

questions.prompt: How many of the four strips in the new zipped pairs are brand new?
hints: The old strips are not thrown away. What happens to them?
Each old strip is given one new partner.
Count the new partners.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two old strips are kept. Each gets one new partner, so two of the four strips are new.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each pair keeps one old strip and gains one new one. DNA copying works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: Two of the four are the old strips, which were kept.
Each old strip gets its own new partner, so there is more than one new strip.

questions.prompt: What makes a DNA strand a template?
hints: Think about what decides each new base.

acceptedIdeas: Its base order fixes the base order of its partner
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because of base pairing, each base in the strand fixes the base opposite it.

choices.label: It is always the longer strand
Its base order fixes the base order of its partner
It can be read only from the left

questions.onCorrect: Its base order fixes its partner's. Each base allows only one partner.

misconceptions.feedback: Both strands are the same length. What matters is the order of their bases.
A strand can serve as a template at any point along its length.

questions.prompt: What are the two joined copies of a replicated chromosome called?
hints: The two copies are attached to each other.
They are identical, like siblings from the same copying.
The name has two words and ends in 'chromatids'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A replicated chromosome has two sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They are identical copies, and they are counted as a single chromosome until they separate.

misconceptions.feedback: Together the two copies are still counted as one chromosome. The question asks for the name of each joined copy.
Homologous chromosomes come from different parents. These two copies come from one chromosome.

questions.prompt: A membrane is permeable to water but not to a dye. 9 dye units are on the left and 3 on the right. How many dye units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Ask which substance the question is about, the water or the dye.
A substance that cannot cross cannot be shared out between the sides.
The dye amounts stay as they began.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dye cannot cross, so its amounts do not change: 9 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: The dye cannot cross, so its amount on each side never changes, however freely the water moves.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share each side would hold if the dye could cross. This membrane does not let it through.
That is the amount on the right, which also stays where it began. The question asks about the left side.
That is the total of both sides. The left side keeps only the amount it began with.

questions.prompt: Two equal rooms are joined by an open door. 20 people start in the left room and 4 in the right, and everyone wanders at random. After a long time, how many people are in the left room?
hints: Does anyone leave the building, or arrive?
Count everyone in both rooms together.
Think about sharing that crowd between two equal rooms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Everyone is still in the building: 20 + 4 = 24. Equal rooms end up with equal crowds: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. People cross both ways, but more leave the crowded room, so the rooms settle at equal numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: That's where the left room started. People keep crossing the door, so the count changes.
That's everyone in the building. The question asks about the left room only.

questions.prompt: Dye is dropped into still water. Overall, where does the dye move?
hints: Which region sends more particles across the boundary between them?

acceptedIdeas: From where it is crowded to where it is not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net movement runs from the more concentrated region to the less concentrated one.

choices.label: From where it is crowded to where it is not
From where it is sparse to where it is crowded
Nowhere, because particles never move

questions.onCorrect: From crowded to sparse. More particles cross that way, so the net movement follows.

misconceptions.feedback: That would make the crowd even more crowded. More particles leave the crowded region than enter it.
Particles move constantly. It is the net movement that settles down, not the particles.

questions.prompt: Why does the total stay the same while solute moves?
hints: Think about where each particle goes.

acceptedIdeas: Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Diffusion moves solute between compartments but does not create or destroy it.

choices.label: Solute is replaced from outside the compartments
Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
The two sides swap their solute exactly

questions.onCorrect: Diffusion only moves solute around. The total is conserved, so you can add the sides first.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing arrives from outside this closed system.
The sides don't swap. Net movement stops once the concentrations match.

questions.prompt: What word describes a membrane that lets a substance cross?
hints: The word starts with per-, meaning through.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane is permeable to a substance if the substance can cross it.

questions.onCorrect: Permeable. Always check what a membrane is permeable to before predicting movement.

misconceptions.feedback: Impermeable means the opposite: nothing can cross.

questions.prompt: Three independent treated pots grow 7 cm, 9 cm and 11 cm. What is the mean growth, in cm?
hints: The mean needs the total of all three measurements.
Add the three growths together.
Divide the total by the number of pots, which is three.
questions.onCorrect: The total is 7 + 9 + 11 = 27 cm, and 27 ÷ 3 = 9 cm is the mean growth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the three pots. The mean divides the total by the number of pots.
That is the largest growth. The mean uses all three pots and divides their total by three.
That is the number of pots. The mean is the total growth divided by it.

questions.prompt: A researcher gives fertiliser only to the plants that already look healthiest. Name the feature of a fair test that this breaks.
hints: Choosing the healthiest plants for the treatment gives the treated group an advantage.
A fair test lets chance decide which plants get the treatment.
The name has two words, and the first is 'random'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Choosing the healthiest plants for the treatment builds a systematic difference into the groups.

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment. Choosing the healthiest plants makes the groups unalike before the treatment begins.

misconceptions.feedback: The test may well have a control. What this choice breaks is the way plants are allocated to the groups.
The number of replicates is a separate matter. The choice of healthiest plants breaks the way plants are allocated to groups.

questions.prompt: Plant A, with fertiliser, grows from 4 cm to 19 cm. Plant B, without it, grows from 12 cm to 22 cm. How many more centimetres did plant A grow than plant B?
hints: Work out each plant's growth separately, as its later height minus its starting height.
Plant A grew from 4 cm to 19 cm, and plant B grew from 12 cm to 22 cm.
Subtract plant B's growth from plant A's growth.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Plant A grew 19 − 4 = 15 cm. Plant B grew 22 − 12 = 10 cm. The difference is 5 cm.

questions.onCorrect: Plant A grew 19 − 4 = 15 cm and plant B grew 22 − 12 = 10 cm, so A grew 5 cm more.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares the final heights, 22 and 19, in the wrong direction. The growth of each plant is its change from where it began.
That is the difference between the starting heights, 12 and 4. The question asks how much more plant A grew.
That is plant A's growth on its own. The question asks how much more it grew than plant B.

questions.prompt: Why compare each group's change instead of its final height?
hints: Think about where each group began.

acceptedIdeas: The groups started at different heights
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Groups that start at different heights can mislead if only final height is compared.

choices.label: Final heights cannot be measured
The groups started at different heights
Change is always larger than final height

questions.onCorrect: The groups started at different heights, so only each group's change shows how much it grew.

misconceptions.feedback: Final heights can be measured. They just do not show how much each group grew.
Size does not decide which measure is fairer. The starting point does.

questions.prompt: Level 3 holds 50 kJ and the transfer efficiency is 10%. How many kJ did level 2 hold?
hints: Level 3 holds one tenth of what level 2 held.
Work backwards from the 50 kJ.
Divide 50 by 0.10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Level 2 held 50 ÷ 0.10 = 500 kJ.

questions.onCorrect: Level 3 holds a tenth of level 2, so level 2 held 50 ÷ 0.10 = 500 kJ.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes a tenth of the 50 kJ, going up a step. The level below held more, not less.
That is the energy at level 3. The level below must have held more than that.
Adding ten percent is not the reverse of taking ten percent. Level 2 held ten times as much as level 3.

questions.prompt: Producers hold 6000 kJ and the transfer efficiency is 10% at each step. How many kJ reach level 3?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Take 10% of the energy twice.
Multiply 6000 by 0.1 twice.
questions.onCorrect: The first step gives 6000 × 0.1 = 600 kJ and the second gives 600 × 0.1 = 60 kJ at level 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2, after one step. Level 3 is a further step on.
That is the energy at level 4, after three steps. Level 3 needs only two.
That subtracts 10% once, which leaves the energy that did not pass on. Each step passes on a tenth.

questions.prompt: A cow eats 120 kilograms of grain and gains 15 kilograms of body mass. How many kilograms of grain does it eat for each kilogram it gains?
hints: Compare the grain eaten with the mass gained.
You want grain per kilogram gained, so the mass gained is what you divide by.
Divide the grain by the mass gained.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 120 kg of grain ÷ 15 kg gained = 8 kg of grain per kg gained.

questions.onCorrect: The cow eats 120 ÷ 15 = 8 kilograms of grain for every kilogram it gains.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grain eaten in total. The question asks how much grain there is for each kilogram gained.
That is the fraction of the grain that became body mass. The question asks for the grain per kilogram gained, which is the reverse.
That is the mass of grain that did not become body mass. The question asks for the grain eaten for each kilogram gained.

questions.prompt: Why is the second 10% taken from the energy at level 2 and not from the original amount?
hints: Each transfer moves energy from one level to the next.

acceptedIdeas: Each transfer starts from the energy that reached the level it leaves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second transfer passes on a share of what level 2 holds.

choices.label: Level 2 gains extra energy from the sun
Each transfer starts from the energy that reached the level it leaves
The original amount is no longer counted

questions.onCorrect: Each step passes on a share of what that level holds, so the shares multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: The original energy is still the source. It has just been reduced by the first transfer.
In this accounting nothing new enters at level 2.

questions.prompt: An enzyme sample makes 9 units of product per minute and its control makes 3 per minute. After 5 minutes, how many more units has the enzyme sample made?
hints: Find how many more units the enzyme sample makes each minute.
The two samples run for the same 5 minutes.
Multiply the extra per minute by the number of minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rates differ by 9 − 3 = 6 per minute. Over 5 minutes: 6 × 5 = 30 more units.

questions.onCorrect: The enzyme sample makes 9 − 3 = 6 more units each minute, so after 5 minutes it is 6 × 5 = 30 units ahead.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the extra per minute. The question asks how many more units there are after 5 minutes.
That is the enzyme sample's whole product over 5 minutes. The control makes some of it anyway.
That is the control's product over 5 minutes. The question asks for the enzyme sample's extra.
Adding the two rates does not measure the enzyme's effect. Subtract the control's rate from the enzyme's.

questions.prompt: How many times faster is beaker B?
hints: Compare the two rates.
How many lots of 4 make 12?
Divide the faster rate by the slower one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so beaker B is three times as fast.

questions.onCorrect: 3 times. The helper changes how fast the reaction runs, and enzymes do exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: That's how much more B makes each minute. 'Times faster' compares by dividing.
That adds the two rates. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A speeds up as it is warmed from 10°C to 40°C. What happens to its rate at 55°C?
hints: Think about what high temperatures do to a folded protein.
A rate falls when the enzyme can no longer bind its substrate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls

choices.label: It rises further
It stays at the rate it had at 40°C
It falls

questions.onCorrect: By 55°C an enzyme like A has begun to lose its shape, and the substrate fits less well.

misconceptions.feedback: Warmth speeds an enzyme up only until its shape starts to change. Beyond that, the active site no longer fits the substrate.
The rate is not fixed. Once the temperature is high enough to change the enzyme's shape, the rate changes with it.

questions.prompt: Name the part of an enzyme where the substrate binds.
hints: It is the notch drawn in the enzyme in the figure.
It is named for what happens there: the enzyme is active at this place.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.

questions.onCorrect: The active site. Its shape and chemistry match the substrate, which is why each enzyme works on so few substances.

misconceptions.feedback: The substrate is what binds. The question asks for the part of the enzyme where it binds.

questions.prompt: Why can't we say that 40°C is the best temperature for every enzyme?
hints: Think about the enzyme's shape.

acceptedIdeas: Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range can differ
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The best temperature depends on the enzyme, and the data only cover the temperatures that were measured.

choices.label: Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range can differ
Every enzyme works best at the same temperature
Temperature never affects enzymes

questions.onCorrect: Each enzyme has its own shape, so its best range differs. Data show only the temperatures tested.

misconceptions.feedback: The two enzymes on the screen do not peak together.
Temperature changes rate in all of these data sets.

questions.prompt: Not all the energy from fuel ends up in ATP. In what form does much of the rest disperse?
hints: Think about why your body stays warm.
It is the form of energy that spreads out as warmth.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy that is not transferred to ATP disperses as heat.

questions.onCorrect: As heat. Respiration transfers part of the fuel's energy to ATP and disperses the rest as warmth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is not what a cell disperses its spare energy as. The form is the one that keeps a mammal's body warm.
ATP is where part of the energy goes. The question asks about the rest, which is not captured in it.

questions.prompt: A cell completely breaks down five glucose molecules using oxygen. How many carbon atoms end up in CO₂?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in the five glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms and all of them end up in CO₂.
Multiply the number of glucose molecules by six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose has six carbon atoms, and all of them end up in CO₂: 5 × 6 = 30.

questions.onCorrect: Five glucose hold 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, and all of them leave in carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.feedback: Six carbon atoms are in a single glucose. Five glucose hold five times as many.
That is the number of glucose molecules. Each one holds six carbon atoms.
Adding 5 and 6 does not count the carbon. Each glucose has six carbon atoms, so multiply.

questions.prompt: Which gas, made when cells use sugar as fuel, do you breathe out?
hints: Think about what leaves your body in every breath out.
It is the gas made from the carbon in the sugar a cell uses.
It is the gas that a plant takes in during photosynthesis.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cells release carbon dioxide when they use sugar as fuel.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. The carbon in the fuel leaves the cell in this gas and is carried out in your breath.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is what a cell takes in to use the fuel. The gas made from the fuel's carbon is a different one.
Water is also made, but it contains no carbon. The question asks for the gas that carries the fuel's carbon away.

questions.prompt: Why can you count the CO₂ by counting the carbon atoms in the fuel?
hints: Think about what happens to atoms in any chemical reaction.

acceptedIdeas: Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms are conserved, so the carbon from the fuel ends up in the products.

choices.label: Carbon atoms are turned into energy
Oxygen supplies the carbon
Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed

questions.onCorrect: Atoms are conserved. The carbon is rearranged into CO₂, so the counts match.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy and atoms are different things. Atoms are never turned into energy in a cell.
Oxygen is a reactant here, but the carbon comes from the fuel.

questions.prompt: In three minutes a sealed jar of organisms loses 9 units of oxygen, and a blank jar with no organisms, set up in the same way, loses 2. How many units did the organisms themselves use?
hints: The blank jar shows a loss that has nothing to do with the organisms.
That loss is also part of the organism jar's total.
Subtract the blank's loss from the organism jar's loss.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 2 = 7 units. The blank's loss is not the organisms' doing.

questions.onCorrect: The blank shows that 2 of the 9 units were lost anyway, so the organisms used 9 − 2 = 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole loss from the organism jar. The blank shows that part of it happened without any organisms.
That is the loss in the blank jar, which has no organisms. The question asks how much the organisms used.
Adding the two losses does not measure the organisms' use. Subtract the blank's loss from the organism jar's.

questions.prompt: A cell has a plasma membrane and DNA, but no nucleus and no mitochondria. What kind of cell is it?
hints: Which cell type keeps its DNA in a nucleoid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No nucleus and no organelles is the bacterial design.

questions.onCorrect: A bacterium. No nucleus and no mitochondria is the bacterial design.

misconceptions.feedback: Animal and plant cells have a nucleus and mitochondria. This cell has neither.

questions.prompt: What should a cell's outer boundary be like?
