hints: What would happen to the food if nothing could get in?

acceptedIdeas: A skin that lets some things through and keeps others out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A cell needs a boundary that lets some things through and keeps others out.

choices.label: A skin that lets some things through and keeps others out
No boundary, so the cell mixes with its surroundings
A sealed wall that lets nothing through

questions.onCorrect: A boundary that lets some things through and holds others back. Cells have exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: A sealed wall would starve the cell and trap its waste.
Without a boundary the cell's contents would drift away and its chemistry would fall apart.

questions.prompt: A cell keeps its DNA inside a nucleus. What kind of cell is it?
hints: Animal and plant cells are this kind.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A cell with a nucleus is eukaryotic.

questions.onCorrect: Eukaryotic. A nucleus holding the DNA is the mark of a eukaryotic cell.

misconceptions.feedback: Bacteria have no nucleus. Look for the cell type that does.

questions.prompt: What does the nucleus's own membrane do for the DNA?
hints: Think about what a membrane does for any compartment.

acceptedIdeas: It keeps most of the DNA enclosed in one compartment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nuclear membrane encloses most of the DNA in one compartment.

choices.label: It makes the DNA copy itself faster
It keeps most of the DNA enclosed in one compartment
It turns the DNA into protein

questions.onCorrect: It encloses the DNA. A membrane-bound compartment is what makes a nucleus a nucleus.

misconceptions.feedback: Copying is done by enzymes. The membrane's job is to enclose.
Proteins are built elsewhere in the cell. The nucleus holds the DNA that carries their instructions.

questions.prompt: Which organelle captures light energy in a leaf cell?
hints: Leaf cells are green because of it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chloroplasts capture light energy.

questions.onCorrect: The chloroplast. It captures light energy for photosynthesis.

misconceptions.feedback: Mitochondria work with fuel, not light.

questions.prompt: A plant is given CO₂ whose carbon atoms are labelled. Name the kind of molecule the labelled carbon ends up in.
hints: The labelled carbon goes where the carbon goes.
The carbon from CO₂ is joined into the product of photosynthesis.
It is the sugar the leaf makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The carbon from CO₂ is built into sugar such as glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Glucose, the sugar. The labelled carbon atoms are built into it.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen gas contains no carbon. The labelled carbon atoms end up in the product that is built from them.
Water contains no carbon, so labelled carbon cannot end up there.

questions.prompt: A leaf makes four glucose molecules. How many water molecules does that use, using the simplified equation?
hints: The simplified equation gives the water used for one glucose.
Each glucose uses six H₂O.
Multiply that number by the four glucose.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose uses six H₂O: 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: Each glucose uses six H₂O, so four glucose use 4 × 6 = 24.

misconceptions.feedback: Six H₂O are used for a single glucose. Four glucose use four times as many.
That is the number of glucose molecules. Each one uses six H₂O.
Adding 4 and 6 does not count the water. Each glucose uses six H₂O, so multiply.

questions.prompt: Where did nearly all of the tree's new mass come from?
hints: How much mass did the soil lose compared with the tree's gain?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of a tree's new mass is built from carbon dioxide in the air and from water.

choices.label: Sunlight itself
The soil
The air and water

questions.onCorrect: The air and water. Plants build their bodies from carbon dioxide and water, not from the soil.

misconceptions.feedback: The soil lost almost nothing, so it cannot account for such a large gain.
Light carries energy, but it adds no atoms to the tree.

questions.prompt: In the overall equation, how many CO₂ molecules go in for one glucose molecule?
hints: Read the number written in front of CO₂.
Find CO₂ on the left-hand side of the equation.
It matches the number of carbon atoms in glucose.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equation starts 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light, so six CO₂ per glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Six. One glucose has six carbon atoms, and each CO₂ brings one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.
That is the number of hydrogen atoms in glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.

questions.prompt: Why does the number of CO₂ molecules equal the number of carbon atoms in the sugar?
hints: Count the carbon atoms inside one CO₂.

acceptedIdeas: Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each CO₂ contains one carbon atom, and every carbon atom in the sugar came from one.

choices.label: Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom
Water supplies the carbon
Light supplies the rest of the carbon

questions.onCorrect: Each CO₂ carries one carbon atom, so counting carbon atoms counts CO₂ molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: Light is energy and has no atoms.
Water contains hydrogen and oxygen only. The carbon comes from the gas.

questions.prompt: A human gamete has 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human body cell have?
hints: The gamete carries one set of chromosomes.
A body cell carries two sets.
Double the number in the gamete.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A body cell is diploid, with two sets: 2 × 23 = 46.

questions.onCorrect: A gamete has one set and a body cell has two, so a human body cell has 2 × 23 = 46 chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number in the gamete, which carries one set. A body cell carries two sets.
That is four sets. A body cell carries two sets, one from each parent.
Three sets is not the normal state of a human cell. A body cell has two sets.

questions.prompt: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. What does meiosis II separate?
hints: Meiosis II works like mitosis.
At that point each chromosome still consists of two joined copies.
The answer is two words, and the first is 'sister'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. Meiosis II separates them as mitosis does, giving four cells in all.

misconceptions.feedback: Those were separated in meiosis I. In the second division the two copies of each chromosome are separated.
Gametes are what results. The question asks which structures are separated.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 12 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does each gamete made from it have?
hints: A gamete is haploid, with one set of chromosomes.
The diploid cell has two sets.
Divide the diploid number by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A gamete is haploid, with half the diploid number: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: A gamete is haploid, with half the diploid number, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6 chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number in the diploid cell. A gamete has only half of it.
That is a quarter of the diploid number. A gamete has half of it, one chromosome from each pair.
Doubling goes the wrong way. Meiosis halves the chromosome number.

questions.prompt: A puppy's first cell has 78 chromosomes, and the egg and the sperm each supplied the same number of them. How many chromosomes does the egg carry?
hints: A new animal's first cell gets chromosomes from two parents.
The egg and the sperm supply equal numbers.
Divide the total by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The egg and sperm each supply half of 78: 78 ÷ 2 = 39.

questions.onCorrect: The egg and the sperm each supply half of the 78, which is 78 ÷ 2 = 39 chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number in the first cell, which has both parents' contributions added together. The egg supplies only its own share.
Doubling goes the wrong way. The egg and sperm together make 78, so each supplies half.

questions.prompt: Why does the chromosome number halve in meiosis I and not in meiosis II?
hints: Think about which relationship is separated in each division.

acceptedIdeas: Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In meiosis I each daughter gets one chromosome from each homologous pair, so the number halves.

choices.label: Meiosis II copies the DNA again
Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
DNA is destroyed in meiosis I

questions.onCorrect: Each cell gets one chromosome from each pair in meiosis I. Meiosis II only separates the copies.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no second copying. Meiosis II divides the existing copies.
No DNA is destroyed. Each chromosome goes to one daughter cell.

questions.prompt: After replication, a cell has 10 DNA molecules. How many chromosomes does it have?
hints: Each chromosome now holds two DNA molecules.
The chromosome count is half the DNA molecule count.
Divide the number of DNA molecules by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each chromosome now holds two DNA molecules, so 10 ÷ 2 = 5 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: After copying each chromosome holds two DNA molecules, so 10 molecules means 10 ÷ 2 = 5 chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of DNA molecules. Each chromosome now holds two of them, so the chromosomes are fewer.
Doubling goes the wrong way. The molecules are twice the chromosomes, so halve the count.
That is the number of molecules in each chromosome. The question asks how many chromosomes there are.

questions.prompt: One cell completes four ideal rounds of division, with every descendant dividing each round. How many cells result?
hints: Each round doubles the number of cells.
Start with one cell and double it once for each round.
Double four times in a row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16.

questions.onCorrect: Each round doubles the count: 1, 2, 4, 8, then 16 cells after four rounds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number after three rounds. A fourth round doubles it again.
That adds 3 each round. Every cell divides, so the count doubles each round.
That is the number of rounds. The question asks for the number of cells.

questions.prompt: How many pages does each student receive?
hints: Each student gets a whole set, not part of one.
How many pages are in one set?
The copy is as long as the original.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each student gets one complete set, which has 5 pages.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Each side gets a full set. Dividing cells copy their chromosomes before sharing them out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total number of pages. Each student gets one set only.
That counts the students. The question asks about pages.

questions.prompt: Why does each sister chromatid count as one DNA molecule?
hints: What did replication copy?

acceptedIdeas: It is one copy of the chromosome's DNA
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each chromatid is one complete copy of the chromosome's DNA molecule.

choices.label: It is one copy of the chromosome's DNA
It is a protein, not DNA
It is half a DNA molecule

questions.onCorrect: Each chromatid is one complete copy. Two chromatids mean two DNA molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: Replication makes complete copies, not halves.
Chromatids are made of DNA with its proteins. The DNA is what is counted.

questions.prompt: A tissue has 8 cells. In one round only half of them divide, and each of those becomes two cells. How many cells are there after that round?
hints: Work out how many of the 8 cells divide.
Each cell that divides becomes two cells.
Add the new cells to the ones that did not divide.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four cells divide into eight, and four do not: 8 + 4 = 12 cells.

questions.onCorrect: Four cells become 8 and four stay as they are, so the tissue has 8 + 4 = 12 cells.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what happens if every cell divides. Only half of them do here.
That is the starting number. The cells that divide add to it.
That is only the number of cells that divide. The others are still part of the tissue, and each dividing cell becomes two.

questions.prompt: A gene has 600 bases. A single substitution changes one of them. How many bases does the mutated gene have?
hints: A substitution swaps one base for another.
Does a swap change the number of bases?
Think about whether any base is added or removed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A substitution swaps one base for another, so the length is unchanged: 600 bases.

questions.onCorrect: A substitution swaps one base for another, so no base is added or lost, and the gene still has 600.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the length after a deletion. A substitution replaces a base and removes none.
That would be the length after an insertion. A substitution replaces a base and adds none.
That is the number of bases that changed. The question asks for the length of the whole gene.

questions.prompt: A mutation arises in one of a parent's skin cells. What is the likely result for the parent's children?
hints: Think about which cells pass DNA to children.
A skin cell is a body cell.

acceptedIdeas: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mutation confined to an ordinary body cell generally does not reach offspring.

choices.label: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
They inherit it only if it is harmful
They inherit it

questions.onCorrect: The children do not inherit it, because the mutation is not in a gamete.

misconceptions.feedback: A mutation in a skin cell stays in that cell and its descendants. It is not in the eggs or sperm that make a child.
Whether a mutation is harmful makes no difference to whether it reaches children. Only a mutation in a gamete can.

questions.prompt: Compare the aligned sequences ACGTAC and TCGAAG. How many positions differ?
hints: Line the two sequences up position by position.
Compare the first letters, then the second, and so on.
Count the positions where the letters differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 1, 4 and 6 differ; the other three agree.

questions.onCorrect: Positions 1, 4 and 6 differ, and the other three agree, so the count is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: Check each position again. One more position has a different letter.
Check each position again. One of the positions you counted has the same letter in both.
That is the length of each sequence. The question asks how many positions differ.

questions.prompt: How many slips are on the page, on average?
hints: How many hundreds of words are on the page?
There is one slip for each hundred words.
Divide the page length by the words per slip.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 words ÷ 100 words per slip = 5 slips.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Even careful copying makes errors at a steady rate, and copying DNA is no different.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many words go by between slips. Count the slips on the whole page.
That is the slips in a single hundred words. The page has more words than that.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from a single DNA substitution alone?
hints: A changed letter does not specify a trait.

acceptedIdeas: Its biological effect needs additional evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Effects depend on sequence context and environment; some substitutions have little detectable effect.

choices.label: It must improve survival
It must be harmful
Its biological effect needs additional evidence

questions.onCorrect: Its effect needs more evidence. A changed base may be harmful, helpful or make no difference.

misconceptions.feedback: Many substitutions have little or no effect, so harm cannot be assumed.
Some help, but a change alone does not show that.

questions.prompt: Do mutations arise because an organism needs them?
hints: Think about whether a mutation can know what a cell needs.
Mutations are changes in DNA that happen by chance.

acceptedIdeas: No, they arise by chance, whether or not they turn out to be useful
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, they arise by chance, whether or not they turn out to be useful

choices.label: Yes, a mutation appears once the environment makes it useful
No, they arise by chance, whether or not they turn out to be useful
Only in bacteria, which change their DNA when a virus attacks them

questions.onCorrect: Whether a mutation helps is decided afterwards, by the environment its carriers live in.

misconceptions.feedback: A mutation is a chance change in DNA and cannot know what a cell needs. Whether it helps is decided only afterwards.
Luria and Delbrück found that resistant bacteria arose at random times before the virus was added, so bacteria do not make the mutations they need either.

questions.prompt: Natural selection acts only on differences that pass from parents to offspring. What word describes such differences?
hints: Think about what has to pass from parents to offspring.
The word describes a difference that can be inherited.
It begins with 'herit'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Heritable differences can be passed on, so selection can change their frequency.

questions.onCorrect: Heritable. Selection can change a population only through differences that offspring inherit.

misconceptions.feedback: A difference that is acquired in one lifetime is not passed on through DNA. Selection needs differences that are inherited.

questions.prompt: How many green beetles are left?
hints: Only the green beetles are eaten.
The birds eat half of them.
Halve the number of green beetles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Half of 16 is 8, so 8 green beetles remain.

questions.onCorrect: 8. One colour is removed faster than the other, so the colours' shares of the population will shift.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many green beetles there were before the birds ate any.
That takes half of the whole meadow. The birds ate only half of the green beetles.

questions.prompt: Why compare percentages instead of counts when the population size changes?
hints: What happens to a count if the population doubles?

acceptedIdeas: A count changes with the size of the population, but a frequency does not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A frequency is a share of the whole, so it can be compared between populations of different sizes.

choices.label: Counts cannot be added
A count changes with the size of the population, but a frequency does not
Percentages are always larger than counts

questions.onCorrect: A share of the whole stays comparable when the population size changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Size has nothing to do with which number is larger. The point is what each one measures.
Counts can be added. The problem is comparing populations of different sizes.

questions.prompt: In a golden meadow, blue beetles fall from 20 of 40 to 8 of 40. What percentage of the beetles is blue afterwards?
hints: The afterwards figure is 8 blue beetles out of 40.
Divide the blue number by the total.
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Blue beetles are 8 of 40, and 8 ÷ 40 × 100 = 20%, down from 50% before.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of blue beetles. The question asks for their share of all the beetles, as a percentage.
That counts the share that is not blue. The question asks for the blue share.
That is the blue share before the change. The question asks for the share afterwards.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 120, with 30 births and 45 deaths. What is its final size?
hints: The new size is the starting size plus births minus deaths.
The starting size is 120.
Add the 30 births and take away the 45 deaths.
questions.onCorrect: The population begins at 120, gains 30 and loses 45, so it ends at 120 + 30 − 45 = 105.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the births but does not take away the deaths. Deaths reduce the population.
That takes away only the births and forgets the starting size. The new size begins from 120.
That is the net change in size, with its sign dropped. The question asks for the final size, which includes the starting 120.

questions.prompt: A population of 6 doubles every round with no limit. How many are there after four rounds?
hints: Each round doubles the population.
Start at 6 and double it once for each round.
Double four times in a row.
questions.onCorrect: Each round doubles the population: 6, 12, 24, 48 and then 96 after four rounds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size after three rounds. A fourth round doubles it again.
That is the size after two rounds. Four rounds need two more doublings.
That adds 6 each round. Doubling means multiplying by two each round, not adding a fixed number.

questions.prompt: A pond is 20 square metres. A patch of lilies covers 1 square metre today and doubles its area every day, with nothing to stop it. On which day from today does the patch first cover more than 20 square metres?
hints: Write the area for each day: day 0 is 1 square metre.
The area doubles every day, so the next area is twice the one before.
Keep doubling until the area is more than 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The area is 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 on days 0 to 4, and 32 on day 5, which is over 20.

questions.onCorrect: The area is 16 on day 4, which is under 20, and 32 on day 5, so day 5 is the first day over 20.

misconceptions.feedback: On day 4 the patch covers 16 square metres, which is not yet more than 20. The next doubling takes it over.
That is the area of the pond, not a number of days. Keep doubling the area day by day and count the days.
Doubling each day is much faster than adding a fixed area each day. Write out the area for each day and watch it double.

questions.prompt: As the pond becomes crowded, what happens to the patch's growth each day?
hints: Think about what happens to the space and nutrients as the patch spreads.
The pond is not unlimited, and a patch that covers more of it has less left to spread into.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It slows down

choices.label: It slows down
It keeps speeding up, as the doubling does
It stays the same each day

questions.onCorrect: As the pond fills there is less space and fewer nutrients, so the patch grows by less each day.

misconceptions.feedback: The growth is not constant once the patch starts to fill the pond, because the space left for it keeps shrinking.
The patch is spreading into a pond whose size does not change, and each day it has less free space left to spread into.

questions.prompt: Why is this population called closed?
hints: Think about what could change the number besides births and deaths.

acceptedIdeas: Individuals enter or leave only by birth and death
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A closed population has no migration, so only births and deaths change its size.

choices.label: Individuals enter or leave only by birth and death
It lives in a closed jar
It has no deaths

questions.onCorrect: No one arrives or leaves. Only births and deaths change the size.

misconceptions.feedback: Deaths do occur. A closed population just has no migration.
Closed describes movement of individuals, not the container.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to show the dominant phenotype?
hints: Draw the four boxes for the cross.
The dominant phenotype shows in any box that has at least one A.
Count those boxes and divide by four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AA, Aa and Aa show the dominant trait: 3 ÷ 4 = 75%.

questions.onCorrect: Three of the four boxes, AA, Aa and Aa, contain A and show the dominant trait, which is 3 ÷ 4 = 75%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that are aa, with the recessive trait. The dominant trait shows in the other boxes as well.
That counts only the Aa boxes. AA offspring show the dominant trait too.
The aa box shows the recessive trait, so not every offspring shows the dominant one.

questions.prompt: Two parents both show the dominant trait, but their child shows the recessive trait. What word describes each parent's genotype?
hints: The child's genotype must be aa to show the recessive trait.
The child received one a from each parent.
Each parent shows the dominant trait, so each must also carry a dominant allele.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each parent must carry one recessive allele without showing it, so each is heterozygous.

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygous. Each parent passed on a, and each shows the dominant trait, so each must be Aa.

misconceptions.feedback: A parent with two dominant alleles could pass on only A. To have an aa child, each parent must carry a as well.
An aa parent would show the recessive trait itself, and both parents here show the dominant one.

questions.prompt: What is the chance, as a percentage, that both coins land heads?
hints: Write out every combination of the two coins.
There are four equally likely combinations.
How many of those four have two heads?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. One of the four is HH: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

questions.onCorrect: 25%. List the equally likely outcomes and count the ones you want. A cross works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one coin. Both coins must land heads.
Each coin could land tails, so both heads is not certain.

questions.prompt: How many boxes does the Punnett square for Aa × Aa have?
hints: Each parent makes two kinds of gamete.
Each box pairs one gamete from each parent.
Multiply the kinds of gamete from the two parents.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each parent makes two kinds of gamete, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 pairings.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Two kinds of gamete from each parent make four equally likely pairings.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the kinds of gamete from one parent. The square pairs gametes from both.
Every pairing of the two parents' gametes gets a box, and that is more than three.

questions.prompt: Why does Aa fill two boxes in the Aa × Aa square?
hints: Think about which parent gives which allele.

acceptedIdeas: A and a can meet in either order, so two boxes give Aa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Aa genotype can be made in two ways, so it fills two of the four boxes.

choices.label: One box is a mistake
Aa is more likely because it is dominant
A and a can meet in either order, so two boxes give Aa

questions.onCorrect: There are two ways to make Aa, so it fills two of the four boxes.

misconceptions.feedback: Dominance affects the trait you see. It does not change how often a genotype forms.
Both boxes are correct. Each shows a different way to make the same genotype.

questions.prompt: In a food web an arrow points from a rabbit to a fox. Which of the two eats the other?
hints: Arrows point from the food to the one that eats it.
Find which organism the arrow ends at.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The arrow runs from food to consumer, so the fox eats the rabbit.

questions.onCorrect: The fox. An arrow points from the food to the organism that eats it.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow starts at the rabbit, so the rabbit is the food. The organism the arrow points to is the one that eats it.

questions.prompt: Which kind of organism returns matter from dead material to the soil and water so that producers can use it again?
hints: Think about what happens to dead plants and animals.
Bacteria and fungi break them down.
The name is built from the verb 'decompose'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Decomposers return matter from dead material to environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Decomposers. They break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil and water.

misconceptions.feedback: Those groups feed on living things or make food from light. The question asks about the organisms that break down dead material.

questions.prompt: A disease kills most of the zooplankton in a pond, and the zooplankton eat the algae. What happens to the amount of algae at first?
hints: Follow the arrow from the algae to the zooplankton.
The zooplankton are the ones that eat the algae.
Ask what losing most of the zooplankton does to the amount of algae that is eaten.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises

choices.label: It rises
It falls
It stays the same

questions.onCorrect: Far fewer algae are being eaten, so their amount rises at first.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow runs from the algae to the zooplankton, so the zooplankton eat the algae, and losing most of them means far less algae is eaten.
The zooplankton were eating the algae, so losing most of them changes how much algae is eaten, and the algae change with it.

questions.prompt: Why do all the routes in a web trace back to a producer?
hints: Where does the first food in the web come from?

acceptedIdeas: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only producers make their own food, so every consumer's energy traces back to them.

choices.label: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
Producers eat all the other organisms
Producers are always the largest organisms

questions.onCorrect: Producers make their own food. Every consumer's energy comes from them, directly or not.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide it. Grass and algae are producers because they make their own food.
Producers are not eaters. The arrows run from them to the consumers.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes at equal pressure hold 9 solute units on the left and 3 on the right. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Only water can cross, so compare the solute concentrations.
Equal volumes mean the side with more units is the more concentrated.
Water moves towards the side with the higher solute concentration.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side holds more solute, so water moves into the left.

questions.onCorrect: The left. It has the higher solute concentration, so water moves in.

misconceptions.feedback: The right side has the lower solute concentration, so water leaves it. Water moves towards the side with more solute.

questions.prompt: A compartment of volume 4 holds 20 units of trapped solute. Water leaves until its volume is 2. What is its concentration now?
hints: The solute stays at 20 while the volume changes.
The volume is now 2.
Divide the amount of solute by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The solute stays at 20: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: Water leaving shrinks the volume to 2 while the 20 units stay put, so the concentration rises from 5 to 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the concentration before the water left, 20 units in a volume of 4. Losing water raises it.
That is the amount of solute, which has not changed. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.
Multiplying gives a number with no meaning here. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.

questions.prompt: A jug holds 6 spoonfuls of syrup in 2 litres of drink. You top it up with water, adding no more syrup, until it holds 4 litres. How many spoonfuls of syrup are there per litre now?
hints: The syrup does not leave the jug, so its amount does not change.
Only the volume has changed, from 2 litres to 4 litres.
Divide the 6 spoonfuls by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The syrup is still 6 spoonfuls. 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 spoonfuls per litre.

questions.onCorrect: The syrup is still 6 spoonfuls, now shared through 4 litres, so the drink holds 1.5 spoonfuls per litre.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the concentration before the top-up, 6 spoonfuls in 2 litres. Adding water changes the volume, so the concentration changes.
That is the number of spoonfuls, which has not changed. The question asks how many there are per litre.
That is the number of litres that were added. The question asks for spoonfuls of syrup per litre of drink.

questions.prompt: You add water to a solution without adding any solute. Does it become more or less concentrated?
hints: The same solute is now spread through more volume.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same solute in more volume gives a lower concentration.

questions.onCorrect: Less concentrated. The same solute is spread through more volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding water adds volume but no solute, so the solute is more spread out.

questions.prompt: A compartment holds 20 solute units in volume 5. Water enters until its volume is 10. What is its concentration now?
hints: The solute cannot cross, so its amount stays at 20.
Only the volume changes, from 5 to 10.
Divide the unchanged amount by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The solute amount is unchanged: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: The 20 units are now spread through a volume of 10, so the concentration has fallen from 4 to 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the concentration before the water entered, 20 units in a volume of 5. After the volume changes, the concentration changes too.
That is the amount of solute, which has not changed. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.
Multiplying gives a number with no meaning here. Concentration is the amount divided by the volume.

questions.prompt: Three independent control pots grow 3 cm, 6 cm and 12 cm. What is the mean growth, in cm?
hints: The mean needs the total of all three measurements.
Add 3, 6 and 12.
Divide the total by the number of pots, which is three.
questions.onCorrect: The total is 3 + 6 + 12 = 21 cm, and 21 ÷ 3 = 7 cm is the mean growth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the three pots. The mean divides the total by the number of pots.
That is the middle value of the three. The mean is the total divided by the number of pots.
That divides the biggest value by the smallest, or something similar. The mean divides the total of all three by three.

questions.prompt: Name the structure that builds proteins in every kind of cell, a bacterium included.
hints: A bacterium has no mitochondria and no nucleus, yet it still makes proteins.
The structure reads instructions copied from the DNA and joins amino acids together.
Its name is a plural, and it appears as a row of dots in the bacterium in the figure.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ribosomes build proteins in bacterial and eukaryotic cells alike.

questions.onCorrect: Ribosomes. Every cell must make proteins, so every cell has them.

misconceptions.feedback: Mitochondria release energy from fuel, and a bacterium has none, though it still makes proteins.
The nucleus stores DNA, and a bacterium has none. The proteins are put together by smaller structures.
DNA holds the instructions and proteins are the product. The question asks for the structure that does the building.

questions.prompt: How many water molecules does a leaf use to make 9 glucose molecules?
hints: The equation uses the same number of water molecules as carbon dioxide molecules.
Each glucose uses six water molecules.
Multiply the number of glucose molecules by six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose uses six H₂O: 9 × 6 = 54.

questions.onCorrect: Each glucose uses six H₂O, so nine glucose use 9 × 6 = 54, the same count as the carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of glucose molecules. Each one uses six water molecules.
Six water molecules are used for a single glucose. Nine glucose use nine times as many.
Adding 9 and 6 does not count the water. Each glucose uses six H₂O, so multiply.

questions.prompt: Enzyme D's rates at 20, 30, 45 and 60°C are 4, 10, 7 and 2 units per minute. Which of the four temperatures is closest to its optimum, in °C?
hints: The optimum is the temperature at which the rate is highest.
Find the largest of the four rates first.
Then read off the temperature at which it was measured.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest rate, 10 units per minute, was measured at 30°C.

questions.onCorrect: The rate climbs to 10 units per minute at 30°C and has fallen to 2 by 60°C, because the enzyme is being denatured.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the highest rate, in units per minute. The optimum is the temperature at which that rate was measured.
At 60°C the rate has fallen to 2, because the enzyme is being denatured, so the optimum lies below it.
At 45°C the rate is 7, and a cooler temperature gave a higher rate than that.

questions.prompt: A leaf with a low supply of CO₂ photosynthesises at a rate of 8 at light level 60, and still at 8 at light level 80. What is limiting its rate at light level 80?
hints: Ask what happened to the rate when the light was raised.
A flat part of the curve means that a factor other than light has become the limit.

acceptedIdeas: Carbon dioxide, which is in short supply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide, which is in short supply

choices.label: Nothing, because the leaf is at the highest rate any leaf can reach
Light, because the leaf needs more of it
Carbon dioxide, which is in short supply

questions.onCorrect: Extra light left the rate unchanged, so light is no longer the limiting factor, and the short supply of carbon dioxide is.

misconceptions.feedback: Raising the light from 60 to 80 left the rate at 8, so more light is not what this leaf is short of.
A leaf given more carbon dioxide goes on speeding up as the light rises, so this one has not reached a ceiling that all leaves share. Its low supply of carbon dioxide holds it back.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the membrane-bound compartment containing most DNA in a typical animal cell?
flashcards.back: The nucleus encloses most of the cell's DNA.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nucleus encloses most of the cell's DNA.

flashcards.front: Which organelle captures light energy in a green leaf cell?
flashcards.back: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; mitochondria serve a different energy role.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; mitochondria serve a different energy role.

flashcards.front: Two equal fixed volumes start with 18 and 6 units of a permeable solute. How many units end up on each side?
flashcards.back: 24 units divide between two equal volumes, giving 12 each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 24 units divide between two equal volumes, giving 12 each.

flashcards.front: What word names net spreading of a freely moving substance down its concentration gradient?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Diffusion produces a net flow down a concentration gradient.

flashcards.front: Name the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane driven by a water-potential difference.

flashcards.front: Name the small molecule commonly used to couple energy release to cellular work.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 × 6 = 24 carbon atoms, one in each CO₂.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Guanine pairs with cytosine (C).

flashcards.front: A cell starts with 10 chromosomes. After replication, each has two chromatids. How many DNA molecules does it contain?

flashcards.front: A starting cell with 8 chromosomes completes normal mitosis and cytokinesis. How many chromosomes does each daughter receive?

A diploid starting cell has 10 chromosomes in 5 pairs. How many chromosomes are in each normal haploid meiotic product?
flashcards.back: A haploid cell has one chromosome from each of the five pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A haploid cell has one chromosome from each of the five pairs.

flashcards.front: What term describes a cell with one chromosome set?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Haploid means one set; diploid means two.

flashcards.front: In an AA × aa cross, what percentage of offspring are heterozygous under the single-gene model?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every offspring receives A from one parent and a from the other, so all are Aa.

flashcards.front: What word describes a genotype with two different alleles at one locus?
flashcards.back: Aa is heterozygous; AA and aa are homozygous.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aa is heterozygous; AA and aa are homozygous.

flashcards.front: What is the general term for a change in DNA sequence?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mutation changes DNA sequence; its effect depends on context.

flashcards.front: Compare GGTACC with GATATC. How many aligned positions differ?
flashcards.back: Positions 2 and 5 differ.

flashcards.front: A population contains 27 blue and 63 gold organisms. What percentage is blue?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Genetic drift changes frequencies through random sampling.

flashcards.back: Carrying capacity depends on the species and current conditions.

flashcards.front: A treatment group grows from 8 to 19 cm; a control from 8 to 15 cm. What is the difference in growth, in cm?

question.prompt: A bacterium makes proteins but lacks a membrane-bound nucleus. Which structure makes its proteins?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bacterial ribosomes synthesise proteins; a nucleus is not required for ribosomes to function.

choices.label: Ribosomes
Chloroplasts
Cell wall

question.prompt: Equal fixed volumes contain 16 and 8 units of a freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (16 + 8)/2 = 12 units per side.

question.prompt: A membrane passes water but blocks sugar. Equal volumes contain 9 sugar units left and 3 right at equal pressure. Which way is initial net water movement?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water moves net toward the higher impermeant-solute concentration, on the left.

choices.label: Left to right
Right to left
No net movement

question.prompt: Adding enzyme increases initial product formation in a matched reaction. What has the enzyme most directly changed?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Catalysis provides a pathway with lower activation energy; it conserves atoms.

choices.label: The activation barrier
The identity of the elements
The total number of atoms

question.prompt: A plant gains carbon in newly synthesised sugars. Which input supplies that carbon?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: CO₂ provides the carbon atoms used to construct sugars.

choices.label: Light
CO₂
O₂

question.prompt: Complete aerobic oxidation of five glucose molecules yields how many CO₂ molecules?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five glucose contain 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, yielding 30 CO₂.

question.prompt: The template is 5′-CGTA-3′. Which is its aligned complementary strand, read left to right?

3′-CGTA-5′
3′-ATGC-5′

question.prompt: A cell with 6 chromosomes completes normal mitosis and cytokinesis. How many chromosomes does each daughter have?

question.prompt: A diploid cell has 4 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes are in each normal haploid meiotic product?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One chromosome from each of four pairs gives four.

question.prompt: In an AA × Aa cross with complete dominance, what percentage of offspring is expected to have the recessive phenotype?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each offspring receives A from the AA parent, so none is aa.

choices.label: One base was substituted
One base was inserted
One base was deleted

choices.label: Natural selection

No possible population change

question.prompt: In the pond web, which arrow indicates the heron eating small fish?

Energy no longer matters
